bus-routes.d: Each bus loops forever over a fixed list of stops. Starting at stop source (not on a bus), return the fewest buses you must ride to reach stop target, or -1.
bus-routes.i: BFS over buses, not stops. Map stop -> buses that visit it; each BFS level = one more bus. Mark buses and stops visited so each route is expanded only once.
k: BFS where nodes are buses, stop->buses map

candy.d: Children stand in a line with ratings. Everyone gets at least one candy and a child with a higher rating than a neighbour must get more than that neighbour. Return the minimum total candies.
candy.i: Two passes: left-to-right satisfies the left neighbour rule, right-to-left satisfies the right one; each child gets the max of the two requirements.
k: Two passes with left[] and right[] arrays
Left pass array + right pass with a running counter

car-fleet.d: Cars at different positions drive toward target at their own speeds. A faster car that catches a slower one joins it and moves at the slower speed. Count how many fleets arrive.
car-fleet.i: Sort by position and walk from the car closest to target. Compute time-to-target; if a car's time is <= the fleet ahead of it, it merges (don't push). Otherwise it starts a new fleet.
k: Sort by position + stack of arrival times

cheapest-flights-within-k-stops.d: Given directed weighted flights, find the cheapest price from src to dst using at most k stops (k+1 edges). Return -1 if impossible.
cheapest-flights-within-k-stops.i: Plain Dijkstra fails because a cheaper path may use too many stops. BFS level by level (stops as the level), relaxing costs; stop expanding after k stops. Bellman-Ford with k+1 rounds is the textbook alternative.
k: BFS by stops with cost relaxation

check-if-array-is-sorted-and-rotated.d: Return true if the array is a non-decreasing array rotated by some amount (possibly zero).
check-if-array-is-sorted-and-rotated.i: Count the 'drops' where nums[i] > nums[(i+1) % n] (circularly). A sorted-and-rotated array has at most one drop.

climbing-stairs.d: You climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. How many distinct ways reach the top?
climbing-stairs.i: ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2): it's Fibonacci. Memoise the recursion, or keep just two variables.

clone-graph.d: Return a deep copy of a connected undirected graph given one of its nodes.
clone-graph.i: DFS with a map original -> clone. Put the clone in the map before recursing into neighbours; the map doubles as the visited set and handles cycles.

coin-change.d: Given coin denominations (unlimited supply) and an amount, return the fewest coins that make the amount, or -1.
coin-change.i: Unbounded knapsack: for coin i either skip it (i-1) or take it and stay at i. Use a big sentinel (1e9) for impossible. 1-D form: dp[a] = min(dp[a], 1 + dp[a - coin]).
k: Bottom-up DP, space-optimised to two rows

coin-change-ii.d: Count the number of combinations (order doesn't matter) of unlimited coins that sum to amount.
coin-change-ii.i: Counting version of unbounded knapsack: ways(i, a) = ways(i-1, a) + ways(i, a - coins[i]). Iterating coins in the outer loop counts combinations, not permutations.

combination-sum.d: Return all unique combinations of distinct candidates (each usable unlimited times) that sum to target.
combination-sum.i: Backtracking with 'take (stay on same index)' or 'skip (move to next index)'. Staying on the same index allows reuse; moving forward only prevents duplicate orderings.
k: Backtracking take/skip, sorted for early pruning

combination-sum-ii.d: Like Combination Sum, but each candidate can be used once and the input may contain duplicates; no duplicate combinations allowed.
combination-sum-ii.i: Sort, then in the for-loop skip candidates[k] == candidates[k-1] when k > start: the same value is never chosen twice at the same depth. Break early once the sum exceeds target.
k: Sort + for-loop backtracking with duplicate skip

concatenation-of-array.d: Return an array of length 2n that is nums followed by nums again.

construct-binary-tree-from-inorder-and-p.d: Rebuild a binary tree (unique values) from its inorder and postorder traversals.
construct-binary-tree-from-inorder-and-p.i: The last postorder element is the root. Its index in inorder (via a HashMap) splits the left and right subtrees; the left subtree size tells you how to split postorder.
k: Recursive split with inorder index map

construct-binary-tree-from-preorder-and-.d: Rebuild a binary tree (unique values) from its preorder and inorder traversals.
construct-binary-tree-from-preorder-and-.i: preorder[preStart] is the root; find it in inorder with a HashMap. leftSize = rootIdx - inStart. Left subtree is preorder[preStart+1 .. preStart+leftSize], right is the rest.

container-with-most-water.d: Given line heights, pick two lines that, with the x-axis, hold the most water. Return that area.
container-with-most-water.i: Two pointers from both ends. Area is limited by the shorter line, so move the shorter one inward: moving the taller one can never give a bigger area.
k: Two pointers, move the shorter side

contains-duplicate.d: Return true if any value appears at least twice in the array.
contains-duplicate.i: Use a HashSet and return as soon as a value is already in it. (Sorting and checking neighbours is O(n log n) with O(1) extra space.)

convert-sorted-array-to-binary-search-tr.d: Turn a sorted array into a height-balanced binary search tree.
convert-sorted-array-to-binary-search-tr.i: Make the middle element the root and recurse on the left and right halves; this keeps the tree balanced.
k: Divide and conquer on the middle element

copy-list-with-random-pointer.d: Deep-copy a linked list whose nodes have both next and random pointers.
copy-list-with-random-pointer.i: Pass 1: create a clone for every node in a map old -> new. Pass 2: set clone.next = map[old.next] and clone.random = map[old.random]. (O(1)-space trick: interleave clones in the original list.)

count-and-say.d: countAndSay(1) = "1"; each next term is the run-length encoding of the previous term (count then digit). Return the nth term.
count-and-say.i: Build each term from the previous one by scanning runs of equal characters and appending count + char.

count-complete-tree-nodes.d: Count the nodes in a complete binary tree, ideally faster than O(n).
count-complete-tree-nodes.i: Simple DFS count is O(n). Faster: if the leftmost and rightmost depths are equal the subtree is perfect, so it has 2^h - 1 nodes; otherwise recurse. That gives O(log^2 n).
